title: 10 — Lakebase and Databricks Apps
html:
10 — Lakebase and Databricks Apps

The one idea: analytics tables are great at scanning millions of rows and bad at saving one click. Workflow screens (review queues, approvals, entitlements) need an operational database. Lakebase puts managed Postgres next to the lakehouse, and Databricks Apps hosts the screens, under the same login and governance.

1. What it is

  • OLTP versus OLAP: online transaction processing (many small reads and writes, row by row) versus online analytical processing (big scans and aggregates). SQL Server serves both moderately. A lakehouse is OLAP. Postgres is OLTP.
  • Lakebase: a managed, serverless PostgreSQL service in Databricks, with instant branching and synced tables between Postgres and Unity Catalog.
  • Databricks Apps: host internal web apps (Python and Node frameworks) inside the workspace, using workspace identity and UC permissions.

2. Why it matters

  • A review queue writes thousands of small decisions a day: accept, reject, escalate. Writing each one to an Iceberg or Delta table would mean thousands of tiny commits. Postgres is built for this.
  • Decisions must still reach the lakehouse, as rows the pipeline applies. Synced tables, or CDC from Postgres, do that.
  • One login and one permission model for screens and data cuts both risk and work.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Where each store fits

Workload Store
Review decisions, entitlement grants, workflow state, app sessions Lakebase (Postgres)
Facts, history, certified products, analytics Iceberg or Delta tables in Unity Catalog
Feeding app screens with Gold data Synced table from UC to Lakebase (read-optimised copy)
Feeding decisions back to pipelines Sync or CDC from Lakebase to UC, then the pipeline applies them 
---
title: Workbench pattern — app, operational database, lakehouse
---
flowchart LR
    U["Analyst"] --> APP["Databricks App<br/>(review screen)"]
    APP --> PG["Lakebase Postgres<br/>decisions, queue state"]
    GOLD["Gold tables (UC)"] -- "synced table" --> PG
    PG -- "sync / CDC" --> DEC["governance.decisions (UC)"]
    DEC --> PIPE["Pipeline applies decisions<br/>(never edits Gold by hand)"]
    PIPE --> GOLD

3.2 Lakebase facts (checked 2026-10-26)

  • Generally available on AWS in February 2026 and Azure on 3 March 2026 (sources differ by a day for AWS). A GCP release note described Lakebase as Beta in June 2026, so availability differs by cloud.
  • Branching: isolated, zero-copy clones of a database for testing, created in seconds.
  • Synced tables: keep Postgres and lakehouse data in sync without hand-built pipelines.
  • The Lakebase Postgres APIs (projects, branches, endpoints, databases, roles, credentials, synced tables, catalogs) became GA on 14 August 2026. Postgres 18 support arrived in June 2026. Lakebase Search (vector and BM25) went GA in September 2026, per secondary sources.

3.3 Databricks Apps

  • Apps run inside the workspace with their own service principal. Users sign in with workspace identity.
  • They read Gold through a SQL warehouse or a synced table, and write decisions to Lakebase.
  • Free Edition currently allows up to three apps per account, and each runs up to 24 hours after a start or redeploy. Older doc versions said one app.
  • I could not confirm a current list of supported frameworks. Check the Apps docs.

4. Working code

This chapter has no runnable code. The pattern in code form (not run: needs a Lakebase instance; connection values are placeholders read from the environment):

# Not run. A minimal decision write from an app, with maker-checker enforced in the database.
import os, psycopg

DDL = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS review_decision (
  decision_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  item_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
  action      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (action IN ('ACCEPT','REJECT','ESCALATE','WAIVE')),
  maker       TEXT NOT NULL,
  checker     TEXT,
  decided_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (action <> 'WAIVE' OR (checker IS NOT NULL AND checker <> maker)));
"""
with psycopg.connect(os.environ["LAKEBASE_DSN"]) as conn:
    conn.execute(DDL)
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO review_decision (item_id, action, maker) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                 ("EXC-101", "ACCEPT", "analyst.a@example.com"))

The CHECK constraint enforces the four-eyes rule for waivers in the database itself, so no screen bug can bypass it.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Writing every click into a Delta or Iceberg table. Thousands of tiny commits. Use Postgres for the workflow state.
  2. Letting the app write Gold. The app writes decisions, and the pipeline applies them.
  3. Rules only in the UI. Enforce maker-checker with database constraints or in the service layer.
  4. Testing migrations on production. Use a Lakebase branch.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

Design the Postgres schema for an exception queue: items, assignments, decisions, SLA timers. Mark which tables sync to Unity Catalog, and which constraint enforces four-eyes on waivers.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is a lakehouse table the wrong place for review-queue state?
  2. What is a Lakebase branch?
  3. How do review decisions reach the certified tables?
  4. When did Lakebase reach GA on Azure?
  5. Where should the four-eyes rule be enforced?

Answers

  1. It is built for large scans and batched commits, not thousands of single-row writes.
  2. An isolated, zero-copy clone of a database, created in seconds for testing.
  3. Through sync or CDC to a decisions table in Unity Catalog, which the pipeline applies. Never by editing Gold directly.
  4. On 3 March 2026.
  5. In the database or service layer as well as the UI, so nothing can bypass it.
